What is C: C is a low-level, statically typed language developed by Dennis Ritchie in 1972. It provides direct memory access, minimal runtime, and is the foundation for most operating systems, embedded systems, and virtually every modern language.
Hello World: Every C program starts execution in `main()`. `#include <stdio.h>` brings in the standard I/O library. `printf()` prints formatted text. `return 0` signals success to the OS.
C Syntax & Structure: C programs consist of functions. `main()` is the entry point. Statements end with semicolons. Blocks are enclosed in braces. `#include` directives include header files. C is case-sensitive and whitespace-insensitive.
Compilation Process: C source code goes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking. `gcc` (GNU C Compiler) is the standard compiler. Use `-o` to name the output, `-Wall` for warnings, `-g` for debug symbols.

gcc -Wall -g -o program program.c
./program
# Or with multiple files
gcc -Wall -o program main.c helper.c -lm
Data Types: Basic types: `int`, `char`, `float`, `double`, `void`. Modifiers: `short`, `long`, `signed`, `unsigned`. `sizeof()` returns bytes. Type sizes vary by platform (int is usually 4 bytes, char is always 1).
Comments: C supports `//` single-line comments (C99+) and `/* */` multi-line comments. Comments are stripped by the preprocessor. Use comments to explain why, not what.

Variables & Assignment: Variables must be declared with a type before use. Naming rules: letters, digits, underscores; cannot start with digit. Convention uses snake_case. Uninitialized local variables contain garbage values.
Constants & Literals: Constants are fixed values that cannot be changed. Use `const` keyword or `#define` preprocessor. Integer, floating-point, character, and string literals. Suffixes: L (long), U (unsigned), F (float).
Scope & Lifetime: Scope determines where a variable is accessible. Block scope `{}`, file scope (global), function scope. Lifetime: automatic (stack) vs static (program duration). Variables shadow outer scopes.
Storage Classes: `auto` (default for locals), `register` (suggest CPU register), `static` (persists lifetime, limits scope), `extern` (declares variable defined elsewhere). `static` on globals limits to file.
Type Qualifiers: `const` makes variable read-only. `volatile` tells compiler value may change externally (hardware registers, signal handlers). `restrict` promises no other pointer aliases the same memory.
Type Conversion: Implicit conversion (type coercion) happens automatically: `int` -> `float` -> `double`. Explicit conversion (casting) uses `(type)` syntax. Promotion rules: values are promoted to the larger type.
typedef: `typedef` creates type aliases for cleaner code. Commonly used with structs, function pointers, and complex types. Doesn't create new types — just aliases.

Arithmetic Operators: Standard math: `+` addition, `-` subtraction, `*` multiplication, `/` division, `%` modulo (remainder). Integer division truncates toward zero. Mixing types causes implicit conversion.
Relational & Logical Operators: Relational: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical: `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), `!` (NOT). C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. Short-circuit evaluation for && and ||.
Bitwise Operators: Manipulate individual bits: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `~` NOT, `<<` left shift, `>>` right shift. Used for flags, hardware control, and performance optimization.

unsigned int a = 5;   // 0101
unsigned int b = 3;   // 0011
unsigned int c = a & b;  // 0001 = 1
unsigned int d = a | b;  // 0111 = 7
unsigned int e = a ^ b;  // 0110 = 6
unsigned int f = a << 1; // 1010 = 10
Assignment Operators: Compound assignments: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `&=`, `|=`, `^=`, `<<=`, `>>=`. More concise and can be more efficient than separate operation and assignment.

int x = 10;
x += 5;   // x = 15
x *= 2;   // x = 30
x %= 7;   // x = 2

unsigned int flags = 0;
flags |= 0x01;  // set bit 0
flags &= ~0x01; // clear bit 0
sizeof, Ternary & Comma: `sizeof` returns size in bytes (type or expression). Ternary `?:` is a compact if-else. Comma `,` evaluates both operands, returns the second. Useful in `for` loops.
Operator Precedence: Precedence determines evaluation order. Postfix > Unary > Multiplicative > Additive > Shift > Relational > Equality > Bitwise AND > XOR > OR > Logical AND > OR > Ternary > Assignment > Comma. Use parentheses to clarify.

if / else if / else: Conditional branching with `if`, `else if`, `else`. Conditions must be in parentheses. C treats 0 as false, non-zero as true. No boolean type in early C — use `<stdbool.h>` for `bool`.
Switch Statement: `switch` branches on integer/enum values. Each `case` must end with `break` to prevent fallthrough. `default` handles unmatched values. C23 allows `switch` on expression with multiple cases per label.
Loops: for, while, do-while: `for` when count is known (init; condition; increment). `while` when condition-based. `do-while` runs body at least once. All loops can be nested. Watch for infinite loops and off-by-one errors.
break & continue: `break` exits the innermost loop or switch immediately. `continue` skips rest of current iteration and goes to next. In nested loops, break only exits the innermost one.
goto & Labels: `goto` jumps to a labeled statement in the same function. Generally discouraged for structured flow, but useful for breaking out of deeply nested loops or centralized error cleanup.
Infinite Loops & Pitfalls: Common loop bugs: off-by-one (`<=` vs `<`), missing braces causing unintended body, using assignment `=` instead of comparison `==`, forgetting increment, and semicolon after `for` or `while`.

Function Declaration & Definition: Functions must be declared before use (prototype) or defined first. Return type, name, parameter list with types. `void` for no return value or no parameters. K&R style is obsolete.
Pass by Value: C passes arguments by value — functions receive copies. To modify variables in the caller, pass pointers. Arrays decay to pointers when passed. Structs are copied unless passed by pointer.
Return Values: Functions return a value matching their declared return type. No value needed for `void`. Returned value can be ignored by caller. Never return pointer to local variable — use `static` or dynamic allocation.
Recursion: A recursive function calls itself. Must have a base case to terminate. Stack memory is used for each call — deep recursion can cause stack overflow. Example: factorial, Fibonacci, tree traversal.
Inline Functions: `inline` suggests the compiler replace function calls with the body code to avoid call overhead (C99). Compiler may ignore. Static inline in headers is common. Modern compilers auto-inline better than programmers.
Variadic Functions: Functions with variable arguments use `<stdarg.h>`: `va_list`, `va_start()`, `va_arg()`, `va_end()`. At least one named parameter is required. No type safety — caller must provide correct types.
main() Arguments: `int main(int argc, char *argv[])` receives command-line arguments. `argc` is argument count (program name is argv[0]). `argv` is array of strings. `getopt()` for parsing flags.

Pointer Basics: Pointers store memory addresses. `&` gets address of variable. `*` dereferences (accesses value at address). `NULL` is a safe pointer value. Always initialize pointers. Size is platform-dependent (4 or 8 bytes).
Pointer Arithmetic: Incrementing a pointer moves to the next element of its type: `ptr + n` adds `n * sizeof(type)` bytes. Arrays and pointers are closely related. Subtraction gives the number of elements between two pointers.
Pointers & Arrays: Array name decays to pointer to first element. `arr[i]` is equivalent to `*(arr + i)`. The `[]` operator works on pointers too. But `sizeof(arr)` differs from `sizeof(ptr)` — arrays remember their size at compile time.
Pointer to Pointer: `int **pp` stores address of an `int*`. Used for dynamic 2D arrays, modifying pointer arguments in functions, and arrays of strings. Can be chained arbitrarily deep.
Void Pointers: `void*` is a generic pointer that can hold any address. Must be cast to a specific type before dereferencing. Used in generic functions like `malloc()`, `qsort()`, `memcpy()`. No pointer arithmetic on void*.
Function Pointers: Function pointers store addresses of functions. Used for callbacks, strategy patterns, and dynamic dispatch. Syntax: `returnType (*name)(params)`. `qsort()` takes a comparator function pointer.
Dynamic Memory Allocation: `malloc()` allocates on heap, `free()` releases it. `calloc()` allocates and zero-initializes. `realloc()` resizes. Always check for NULL return. Free to avoid leaks. Include `<stdlib.h>`.
Memory Leaks & Debugging: A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is never freed. Tools: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`), leak sanitizer. Common issues: forgetting to free, losing the pointer, double free, use-after-free.

One-Dimensional Arrays: Contiguous memory blocks of the same type. Fixed size determined at compile time. Index from 0. No bounds checking — buffer overflows are dangerous and a common security vulnerability.
Multidimensional Arrays: Arrays of arrays stored in row-major order. `int matrix[rows][cols]`. Access with `matrix[r][c]`. Can be passed to functions with all dimensions except first specified.
Array Initialization & Bounds: Arrays can be initialized with `= {values}`. Designated initializers (C99): `int arr[5] = {[0]=1, [4]=5}`. C has no runtime bounds checking — accessing out of bounds causes undefined behavior: crashes or security holes.
Strings as char Arrays: C strings are null-terminated char arrays (`\0` marks end). String literals are `char*` pointing to read-only memory. Always ensure buffer is large enough for the null terminator.
String Library: `<string.h>` provides: `strlen()` (length), `strcpy()` (copy), `strncpy()` (bounded copy), `strcat()` (append), `strncat()` (bounded append), `strcmp()` (compare), `strchr()` (find char), `strstr()` (find substring). Always prefer bounded versions.
Array of Strings: An array of strings is a 2D char array or array of char pointers. `char names[5][20]` — fixed size. `char *names[5]` — flexible, each string can differ in length. Both have different memory layouts.
Character Classification: `<ctype.h>` provides: `isalpha()`, `isdigit()`, `isalnum()`, `isspace()`, `islower()`, `isupper()`, `tolower()`, `toupper()`. Functions work with `int` (EOF-safe). Very efficient — lookup-table based.

Structs: Structures group related data of different types. Define with `struct`. Access members with `.` (dot) operator. Use `->` with pointers to structs. Structs can be copied by assignment.
Unions: Unions store different types in the same memory location (size = largest member). Only one member can hold a value at a time. Useful for variant types, register access, and memory-efficient design. Type punning is common but can be undefined behavior.
Bit Fields: Bit fields pack multiple values into a single integer, specifying exact bits. Used in device drivers, network protocols, and embedded systems. Can't take address of a bit field. Order and alignment are implementation-defined.
enum: Enums define named integer constants (default: 0, 1, 2...). Can specify explicit values. Enums improve code readability and type safety (some compilers warn on switch missing cases). C23 allows `enum` with type specifier.
Struct Padding & Alignment: Compilers may add padding bytes between struct members for alignment. Reorder members from largest to smallest to minimize padding. `offsetof()` from `<stddef.h>` gets member offset. Packed structs with `__attribute__((packed))`.
Flexible Array Members: A struct can have an incomplete array as its last member (C99). Allows variable-length data without pointers. The struct is allocated with extra space for the array. Common in network protocols and variable-length records.
Nested & Self-Referential Structs: Structs can contain other structs as members. Self-referential structs (containing pointer to same type) are used for linked data structures: linked lists, trees, graphs. Forward declaration with `struct Name;`.

Opening & Closing Files: `fopen()` opens a file: `r` read, `w` write (truncates), `a` append, `r+` read/write, `w+` read/write (truncates), `a+` read/append. `fclose()` closes. Always check return value for NULL. Binary mode: append `b` (e.g. `rb`, `wb`).
Reading & Writing Text: Character: `fgetc()`, `fputc()`. Line: `fgets()` (safe, includes newline), `fputs()`. Block: `fread()`, `fwrite()`. `fgets()` reads at most n-1 chars and adds null terminator. `getline()` is POSIX, not standard C.
Formatted I/O: `fprintf()` writes formatted output to a file. `fscanf()` reads formatted input from a file. Format specifiers: `%d` int, `%f` float, `%s` string, `%c` char, `%x` hex. `sscanf()` / `sprintf()` work with strings.
Binary I/O: `fread()` and `fwrite()` read/write raw binary data. Parameters: pointer to data, size of each element, count, file pointer. Binary files are more compact and precise but not portable across endianness. Use `"rb"` / `"wb"` modes.
File Positioning: `fseek(fp, offset, whence)` moves file position: `SEEK_SET` (beginning), `SEEK_CUR` (current), `SEEK_END` (end). `ftell()` returns current position. `rewind()` resets to beginning. `feof()` checks for end-of-file.
Error Handling: File operations set `errno` on failure. `perror()` prints a descriptive error message to stderr. `strerror()` returns the error string. `ferror()` checks if a file stream has an error. Always check return values of I/O functions.

Macros (#define): The preprocessor runs before compilation. `#define` creates macros (constants or function-like). Use parentheses to avoid precedence bugs. No type checking. Convention: UPPER_CASE names.

#define PI 3.14159
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
#define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))

printf("%f\n", SQUARE(5 + 1));  // (6*6) = 36
printf("%d\n", MAX(3, 7));
Conditional Compilation: `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#else`, `#elif`, `#endif` control which code gets compiled. Used for platform-specific code, debug builds, feature toggles. `defined()` operator works in `#if`.
Header Files & Guards: Header files (`.h`) declare functions, macros, and types. Use include guards (`#ifndef`) to prevent double inclusion. `#pragma once` is a modern alternative (non-standard but widely supported).
#pragma & #error: `#error` emits a compiler error with a custom message — stops compilation. `#pragma` provides compiler-specific instructions: `#pragma once` (header guard), `#pragma pack(push, 1)` (packing), `#pragma GCC optimize`. Non-standard.

#ifndef REQUIRED_FEATURE
    #error "REQUIRED_FEATURE must be defined"
#endif

#pragma once  // modern header guard
#pragma pack(push, 1)  // pack structs tightly
#pragma GCC optimize("O3")
Predefined Macros: Standard predefined macros: `__FILE__` (current file), `__LINE__` (current line), `__DATE__` (compilation date), `__TIME__` (compilation time), `__STDC__` (1 if standard C), `__STDC_VERSION__` (C version: 199901L, 201112L, 202311L).
Stringification & Token Pasting: `#` converts macro parameter to string literal. `##` concatenates two tokens into one. Useful for generating repetitive code patterns and creating type-generic macros.
Variadic Macros: Macros with variable arguments using `__VA_ARGS__` (C99). Named variadic argument in C23 (`__VA_OPT__` for trailing comma handling). Useful for debug logging and generic printing.

stdlib.h Utilities: `atoi()` / `atol()` / `atof()` parse strings to numbers. `itoa()` is non-standard — use `sprintf()`. `rand()` / `srand()` for pseudo-random numbers. `qsort()` for sorting. `abs()` / `labs()` for absolute value. `div()` / `ldiv()` for quotient and remainder.
math.h Functions: Mathematical functions: `sqrt()`, `sin()`, `cos()`, `tan()`, `asin()`, `acos()`, `atan2()`, `pow()`, `exp()`, `log()`, `log10()`, `floor()`, `ceil()`, `fabs()`, `fmod()`. Link with `-lm`. Angles in radians.
time.h Functions: `time()` gets current time. `clock()` gets CPU time. `difftime()` calculates difference. `strftime()` formats time. `localtime()` / `gmtime()` convert to struct. `mktime()` converts back. `clock_gettime()` for nanosecond precision (POSIX).
assert.h & setjmp.h: `assert(expr)` aborts if expr is false (debug builds). Disable with `#define NDEBUG`. `setjmp()` / `longjmp()` provide non-local jumps (like try/catch). Save state with `jmp_buf`. Limited, use sparingly — complicates resource cleanup.
signal.h Handling: `signal()` sets a handler for OS signals: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGTERM (termination), SIGSEGV (segfault), SIGFPE (divide by zero). Handler must be `void handler(int sig)`. Some signals (SIGKILL, SIGSTOP) cannot be caught.
stddef.h & Limits: `<stddef.h>`: `size_t`, `ptrdiff_t`, `NULL`, `offsetof()`. `<limits.h>`: integer limits (INT_MIN, INT_MAX, LONG_MAX, CHAR_BIT). `<float.h>`: floating limits (FLT_MAX, DBL_EPSILON). `<stdint.h>`: fixed-width types (int32_t, uint64_t).

Linked Lists: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node points to the next. Singly linked: `next` pointer. Doubly linked: `prev` and `next`. Operations: insert, delete, traverse, search. O(1) insert/delete given pointer, O(n) access by index.
Debugging with GDB: GDB is the GNU debugger. Compile with `-g` for debug symbols. Commands: `run`, `break`, `next`, `step`, `print`, `backtrace`, `watch`, `continue`. Set breakpoints on functions or lines. Inspect variables and memory.

# Compile with debug symbols
gcc -g -o program program.c

# GDB commands:
# gdb ./program
# (gdb) break main
# (gdb) run
# (gdb) print x
# (gdb) next
# (gdb) continue
# (gdb) backtrace
# (gdb) quit
Memory Debugging (Valgrind): Valgrind detects memory leaks, invalid accesses, and use-after-free. Run with `valgrind ./program`. Tools: `memcheck` (default), `callgrind` (profiling), `helgrind` (race conditions). Focus on errors = definitely lost bytes.

# Compile with -g for better output
gcc -g -o program program.c

# Check for memory errors
valgrind --leak-check=full ./program

# Typical output:
# HEAP SUMMARY:
#     definitely lost: 40 bytes in 2 blocks
# ERROR SUMMARY: 3 errors
Build Systems (Make): Make automates compilation. Rules: `target: dependencies`, then tab-indented commands. Variables: `CC=gcc`, `CFLAGS=-Wall`. Automatic variables: `$@` (target), `$<` (first dep), `$^` (all deps).

CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 -g
LDFLAGS = -lm

program: main.o helper.o
	$(CC) -o $@ $^ $(LDFLAGS)

main.o: main.c helper.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $<

helper.o: helper.c helper.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $<

.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f *.o program
Multithreading (pthreads): POSIX threads (`<pthreads.h>`) create concurrent execution. `pthread_create()`, `pthread_join()`, `pthread_mutex_lock/unlock()`, `pthread_cond_wait/signal()`. Data races cause undefined behavior. Always synchronize shared data.
Network Programming (Sockets): Berkeley sockets (`<sys/socket.h>`) for networking. Steps: `socket()`, `bind()`, `listen()`, `accept()` (server) or `connect()` (client). `send()` / `recv()` for data. Use `inet_pton()` for IP addresses. Compile with `-lsocket` on some systems.
Atomics & _Generic (C11): `<stdatomic.h>` (C11) provides portable atomic operations: `atomic_int`, `atomic_store()`, `atomic_load()`, `atomic_fetch_add()`, `atomic_compare_exchange_weak()`. `_Generic` (C11) enables type-generic macros like built-in overloads.

Interactive I/O (getchar/putchar): K&R-style character I/O with `getchar()` and `putchar()`. EOF is a macro (-1 on most systems). Ctrl+D (Unix) / Ctrl+Z (Windows) sends EOF. `getchar()` returns `int`, not `char`, to accommodate EOF. Classic book-copying program.
Low-Level I/O (UNIX System Interface): `<unistd.h>` provides `read()`, `write()`, `open()`, `close()`, `lseek()`. Lower-level than stdio — no buffering, direct file descriptors (ints). Used in systems programming, signal handlers, and performance-critical code. K&R Chapter 8 covers this.
Storage Allocator (K&R Chapter 8): K&R builds a `malloc()`-like allocator using a free list of headers. Each block has a header with size and pointer to next free block. `sbrk()` grows the program break. Real allocators are more sophisticated (thread caches, slab allocators, buddy system).
Complex Declarations (Right-Left Rule): Read C declarations spirally: start at identifier, go right, then left, then right again (spiral rule). `int *(*fp)(int)` is pointer-to-function taking int returning pointer-to-int. Practice with `signal()`: `void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int)`.
Variable-Length Arrays (C99): VLA syntax: `int arr[n]` where `n` is not a compile-time constant. Memory on stack (auto duration). `sizeof` on VLA computed at runtime. No VLA in file scope or structs. Support is optional in C11 (most compilers still provide it).
Complex Numbers (C99): `<complex.h>` provides `complex` type, `I` (imaginary unit), `creal()`, `cimag()`, `cabs()`, `carg()`, `conj()`, `csqrt()`, `cexp()`. Types: `float complex`, `double complex`, `long double complex`. Link with `-lm`.

Defensive Programming: From Learn C the Hard Way: always check return values, validate pointers before dereferencing, assert invariants in debug builds, and enable all compiler warnings. Use `const` for read-only parameters. Never trust user input or buffer sizes.
Three Common Bugs: Learn C the Hard Way drills these: 1) Off-by-one: loop runs one iteration too many/few. 2) Buffer overflow: writing past allocated space. 3) Use-after-free: accessing freed heap memory. Detect with `-fsanitize=address` and Valgrind.
Safe String Handling: C string functions are inherently unsafe. Prefer bounded versions: `strncpy()`, `strncat()`, `snprintf()` (always null-terminates). For POSIX: `strlcpy()` / `strlcat()`. Better yet, use a string struct with explicit length field.
Pointer Pitfalls: From Absolute Beginner's Guide: 1) Uninitialized pointers hold garbage — always init to NULL. 2) Dangling pointers reference freed memory — NULL after free. 3) Null dereference crashes. 4) Pointer arithmetic past bounds is UB. 5) Alignment violations on cast.
Debugging Strategies: Layer your approach: 1) Compiler warnings (`-Wall -Wextra`). 2) `assert()` to catch invariants. 3) `printf()` / `fprintf(stderr)` for tracing. 4) GDB for interactive debugging. 5) Valgrind for memory leaks. 6) AddressSanitizer for fast memory checking.
Working with Multiple Files: Split code across `.h` (declarations with include guards) and `.c` (definitions). `static` functions/variables are file-private. `extern` references names defined in other files. Compile all `.c` files and link them into one executable.

malloc/free Basics: Dynamic memory allocation in C uses malloc (allocate), calloc (allocate + zero-init), realloc (resize), and free (deallocate). malloc returns void* to the allocated memory, or NULL on failure. Always check the return value. free releases memory back to the heap. Include <stdlib.h>. Memory from malloc is uninitialized.
Memory Layout (Stack vs Heap): Process memory is divided into segments: text (code), data (initialized globals), bss (uninitialized globals), heap (dynamic allocation), stack (local variables, function calls). Stack grows downward, heap grows upward. Each thread has its own stack. Stack allocation is fast but limited. Heap is flexible but slower and requires manual management.
Memory Leaks & Valgrind: A memory leak occurs when allocated memory is never freed. Causes: lost pointer, forgotten free, circular reference. Valgrind detects leaks: valgrind --leak-check=full ./program. ASAN (AddressSanitizer) is a compile-time alternative: -fsanitize=address. Best practices: free in the same scope as malloc, use guard patterns, avoid re-assigning pointer before free.
Custom Allocators (Arena): Arena allocators allocate a large block once and sub-allocate from it. Fast allocation (pointer bump), bulk deallocation (reset arena). No per-allocation free needed. Ideal for per-frame or per-request allocations. Simple implementation: aligned pointer bump with remaining size check.

POSIX Threads (pthreads): POSIX threads (pthreads) provide the standard threading API on Unix systems. pthread_create spawns a thread, pthread_join waits for completion. Thread functions return void*. Compile with -pthread. Each thread has its own stack but shares the heap. Thread IDs are opaque (pthread_t). Detach threads with pthread_detach.
Mutexes & Condition Variables: Mutexes prevent race conditions by serializing access to shared data. pthread_mutex_t with lock/unlock. Condition variables (pthread_cond_t) enable thread signaling: wait (block until signaled), signal (wake one), broadcast (wake all). Always check the predicate in a while loop after wait (spurious wakeups). Initialize with PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER.
Atomic Operations: Atomic operations complete without interference from other threads. C11 provides <stdatomic.h> with atomic_int, atomic_store, atomic_load, atomic_fetch_add, etc. Atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) enables lock-free data structures. Memory ordering: memory_order_relaxed, acquire, release, seq_cst. Avoid data races without mutex overhead.
Thread Pool Pattern: A thread pool reuses a fixed number of threads to execute tasks from a queue. Reduces overhead of creating/destroying threads. Worker threads loop waiting for tasks. Tasks are function pointers with void* arguments. Synchronize with mutex and condition variable. Clean shutdown with poison pill or flag.
